name: Multi-field, vector and tensor volume visualization
text:
# Multi-field, vector and tensor volume visualization


## Overview
This family encompasses techniques for visualizing multi-component data fields—specifically vector, tensor, and complex-valued fields—within a volume rendering context [G]. It solves the problem of representing directional, anisotropic, or phase-dependent information that scalar volume rendering cannot convey [G]. It sets itself apart from [Classification and transfer functions](38-classification-and-transfer-functions.md) by mapping non-scalar data attributes (direction, magnitude, phase) to visual properties, and from [Illustrative and non-photorealistic volume rendering](40-illustrative-and-non-photorealistic-volume-rendering.md) by focusing on geometric or color-based encoding of field structure rather than artistic style [G].

## Shared principles
All methods evaluate a mapping function $M(\mathbf{x})$ at sample points $\mathbf{x}$ within the volume to produce visual attributes [G]. The core mechanism involves sampling the multi-component data field at $\mathbf{x}$, decomposing or normalizing the value (e.g., extracting magnitude, direction, eigenvalues, or phase), and applying a transfer function or geometric construction to map these features to rendering parameters such as color, opacity, or [primitive geometry](#6264-primitive-geometry.md) [G].

## Subtopics

### [Domain Colouring](1833-domain-colouring.md)
[Domain Colouring](#1833-domain-colouring.md) maps complex numbers to colors using a cyclic colormap scaled by a degree parameter and brightness. It solves the problem of visualizing the phase and magnitude of complex-valued fields, such as spin orientation. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Line Glyphs](2569-line-glyphs-for-vector-field-visualization.md) by providing a dense, pixel-wise color field rather than discrete geometric primitives.

### [Line Glyphs for Vector Field Visualization](2569-line-glyphs-for-vector-field-visualization.md)
[Line Glyphs](#2569-line-glyphs-for-vector-field-visualization.md) represent vector fields by line segments, with orientation matching the vector and length/color determined by magnitude. It is distinguished from sibling methods like [Arrow Glyphs](2663-arrow-glyphs-for-vector-field-visualization.md) by its extreme computational efficiency and memory footprint, allowing for millions of glyphs, but suffers from ambiguity regarding vector direction and 3D orientation due to the lack of shading.

### [Arrow Glyphs for Vector Field Visualization](2663-arrow-glyphs-for-vector-field-visualization.md)
[Arrow glyphs](#2663-arrow-glyphs-for-vector-field-visualization.md) resolve the direction ambiguity inherent in line-based vector field visualizations by using arrow-shaped primitives that explicitly encode flow direction. Unlike [Line Glyphs for Vector Field Visualization](2569-line-glyphs-for-vector-field-visualization.md), which suffer from orientation ambiguity, arrow glyphs use triangular faces to allow for 3D shading and clear directional cues. This method is implemented entirely on the GPU to avoid CPU-GPU data transfer, resulting in performance approximately 2x faster than line glyphs (about 10 ms for typical scenes) due to the larger visual size of arrows allowing for lower sampling density.

### [Diffusion Tensor Visualization using Random Field Correlation](3441-diffusion-tensor-visualization-using-random-field-correlatio.md)
A volume rendering method that visualizes diffusion tensor fields by correlating a random noise field anisotropically using the diffusion tensor, preserving high-frequency components in transversal directions while smearing noise in the direction of greater diffusivity.

### [Stream Lines](4796-stream-lines.md)
Visualization of vector fields by computing trajectories of mass-less particles ([stream lines](#4796-stream-lines.md)) seeded at specific locations, using an integrator to advance the particle position.

### [Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) Visualization](5713-diffusion-tensor-imaging-dti-visualization.md)
An MRI based acquisition modality yielding 3x3 symmetric diffusion tensors as its native measurement quantity.

### [Multi Field Visualization](6557-multi-field-visualization.md)
Combines multiple field datasets (e.g., density, velocity, temperature) into a single visual representation for previewing and debugging simulation data. Solves verification of multi-component data without full rendering overhead. Choose for interactive simulation debugging.

### [Multi-field Visualization Combination](7061-multi-field-visualization-combination.md)
A visualization strategy combining volumetric scalar fields (object volume) with vector field geometry (glyphs and streamlines from optical flow) to convey both object location and motion status.

### [Error Metric for Vector Fields](7084-error-metric-for-vector-fields.md)
An [error metric for vector fields](#7084-error-metric-for-vector-fields.md) defined by a weighted sum of individual error metrics for parameters such as vector magnitude, gradient, curl, and divergence.

### [Vector Topology Analysis](7694-vector-topology-analysis.md)
A technique to analyze vector field topology based on [critical point classification](#7694-vector-topology-analysis.md) to capture global features of a flow field.

### [Helicity Visualization](8393-helicity-visualization.md)
Visualizing helicity, a scalar value calculated as the dot product of velocity and vorticity, to identify vortices.

### [Shape Space (Tensor Eigenvalue Space)](8885-shape-space-tensor-eigenvalue-space.md)
A vector space spanned by the three eigenvalues of a tensor, where tensor shape is represented by a point with coordinates called shape descriptors.

### [Directional Histogram](8888-directional-histogram.md)
A histogram analyzing the distribution of principal shear directions or eigenvectors projected onto a unit sphere.

### Radial Colormap Visualization
A direct multivariate volume rendering technique where voxels are mapped to a radial colormap based on the values of their multiple channels, allowing visualization of cross-channel interactions and phase/composite identification [S1]. Map each voxel to the radial colormap according to the values of its channels: a voxel high in channel A appears close to the node for A; a voxel high in channel B appears close to the node for B; a voxel containing a mixture of channels appears in between the respective nodes [S1]. Plot a subsampled distribution of voxels within the display to provide a general idea of the voxel distribution relative to the radial colormap [S1]. The radial colormap has distinct nodes corresponding to each channel (e.g., Ce, Gd) in the multivariate dataset [S1]. Used in the RadVolViz research application and the MultivariateView prototype for visualizing multivariate volume datasets such as the MIEC dataset and medical datasets (knee sarcoma) [S1].

### Multivalued Volume Error Metric
A single error metric for multivalued volume data (multiple scalar and/or vector fields) used for view-dependent visualization decisions [S2]. Defined as $E_m(T) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} b_i E_{s,i}(T) + \sum_{i=1}^{l} b_{k+i} E_{v,i}(T)$ where $k$ is the number of scalar fields, $l$ is the number of vector fields, $E_{s,i}$ is the error for the i-th scalar field, $E_{v,i}$ is the error for the i-th vector field, and $b_i$ are normalization coefficients [S2]. The coefficients are $b_i = \frac{1}{v_{\delta,i}^2 \beta}$ where $v_{\delta,i} = |v_{max,i} - v_{min,i}|$ is the range of the i-th error component, and $\beta$ is the power used in the function $g$ [S2]. Coefficients $b_i$ act as normalization coefficients to make the influence of all scalar and vector fields equal [S2].

### Candy Cane Visualization
A two-field visualization technique where enstrophy defines the opacity and the [Seed LIC](#8864-seed-line-integral-convolution.md) texture of the vorticity field defines the color, creating vortex tube structures resembling '[candy canes](#8029-candy-cane-visualization.md)' [S3]. Calculate the enstrophy field ($\epsilon = |\omega|^2$) from the vorticity field [S3]. Generate a Seed LIC texture for the vorticity field to convey directional structure [S3]. Map enstrophy values to opacity using a transfer function [S3]. Map the Seed LIC texture values to color [S3]. Render the volume using [direct volume rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) with the defined transfer functions [S3].

### Multi-variate Volume Rendering
A rendering approach that handles multiple data fields (e.g., temperature and density) simultaneously, often using multi-variate transfer functions [S4, unofficial].

### Vector Field Polar Coordinate Mapping
A representation of vector fields in polar coordinates (magnitude, azimuth, elevation) to map vector properties to visual parameters (opacity, hue, saturation) [S5, unofficial]. Designate the free stream velocity direction as the zero direction vector (axis) [S5, unofficial]. Calculate the azimuth (rotational) angle around the free stream vector [S5, unofficial]. Map the azimuth angle to Hue. The alignment is arbitrary; the y-axis direction was used as zero in the implementation [S5, unofficial]. Calculate the elevation (upstream to downstream) angle the field vector makes with the free stream vector [S5, unofficial]. Map the elevation angle to Saturation. Vectors parallel to free stream are nearly [gray](#10042-gray.md) (unsaturated); vectors 180 degrees to free stream are maximally saturated [S5, unofficial]. Map the magnitude of the vector to Opacity [S5, unofficial]. The free stream velocity direction is selected as the axis for zero direction [S5, unofficial].

### Velocity Component Visualization
Visualizing specific components of the velocity field (e.g., x-component) to identify flow separation and reversal [S5, unofficial]. Map the smallest x velocity values (including negative values) to cyan and high opacity [S5, unofficial]. Map the largest x velocity components to yellow and near transparency [S5, unofficial].

### Continuous Indexed Points for Multivariate Volume Visualization
A technique to improve multivariate volume visualization by representing linear structures in parallel coordinates to encode local correlation of multivariate volume data using [continuous indexed points](#8878-continuous-indexed-points-for-multivariate-volume-visualizat.md) [S6]. Perform local linear fitting in the spatial neighborhood of each volume sample using [principal component analysis](#6565-principal-component-analysis-pca.md), accelerated by hierarchical spatial data structures [S6]. Visualize the local linear information as continuous indexed points in parallel coordinates, which is a density representation of indexed points in a continuous domain [S6]. Utilize both 1-flat and 2-flat indexed points to identify correlations between two variables and three variables, respectively [S6]. Apply an interactive occlusion [shading model](#837-shading-models.md) to facilitate good spatial perception of the volume rendering of volumetric correlation characteristics [S6]. Support interactive exploration using specifically designed multivariate transfer function widgets working in the image plane of parallel coordinates [S6].

### Shape Space Scatterplot
A 2D plot depicting the relation between two scalar invariants, specifically principal stresses, to quantify normal and shear stresses [S7, book]. Sort the three principal stresses in descending order: σ1 ≥ σ2 ≥ σ3 [S7, book]. Plot σ1 on the x-axis and σ3 on the y-axis, dividing the plot into four quadrants (A, B, C, D) [S7, book]. Apply a sign-preserving logarithmic mapping to the eigenvalues: f(σi) = log(σi + 1) for σi ≥ 0, and f(σi) = −log(1 − σi) for σi < 0 [S7, book]. Linearly map the results of the logarithmic mapping to the range [-1, 1] [S7, book]. Unlike standard logarithmic mappings that require positive domains, this method preserves signs to distinguish between positive (tensile) and negative (compressive) invariants [S7, book].

## Background
The visualization of vector and tensor fields is a fundamental problem in scientific visualization, arising in fluid dynamics, electromagnetism, and medical imaging (specifically Diffusion Tensor Imaging) [G]. Early methods relied on glyph-based approaches (arrows, lines) for their intuitive geometric representation [G]. As computational power increased, GPU-based implementations allowed for dense glyph rendering [G]. Color-based methods, such as domain coloring for complex fields, provide a dense alternative to glyphs [G]. The integration of these techniques into [volume rendering pipelines](#1318-volume-rendering-pipeline.md) allows for the simultaneous visualization of scalar context and vector/tensor structure [G].
